description: Space Cadet is hosting a team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, bringing together students interested in astronomy, space exploration, and technology to tackle real-world challenges using creativity, research, and coding. Through collaboration and hands-on problem-solving, members will develop innovative solutions while exploring the possibilities of space science and engineering.
summary:
Welcome to Space Cadet’s Martian Map Survival Guide! We created an interactive Mars exploration website where users can navigate the Red Planet using a 3D animated Mars model and a controllable spaceship. Our project focuses on the Jezero Crater region, using map imagery and Digital Terrain Model (DTM) data from NASA to build interactive 3D terrain maps that reveal the region's elevation and surface features.

Beyond exploration, our website includes a survival guide that introduces the potential dangers of Mars and explains how astronauts can prepare for life in its harsh environment with quizzes. We also developed interactive simulations that calculate mission range based on available resources, such as fuel and food, and help users plan routes across Martian terrain by considering travel distances, resource limits, and potential hazards. Through these features, we aim to make Mars exploration more accessible, engaging, and realistic while showing how NASA's data can support future human missions.
details:
What it does

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is an interactive website that turns real NASA orbital data into tools for exploring Mars and planning safe travel in Jezero Crater. It has four connected parts that go from the whole planet down to a single rover route. In the 3D Mars Interactive Simulator, visitors fly a spaceship around Mars with the W, A, S, D keys, and clicking a landmark such as Western Breach or Perseverance flies to it and opens a card with a description and a real image. The 3D Jezero Crater Interactive Map is a detailed terrain model built from NASA’s HiRISE and CTX elevation data, showing the crater’s real rim, inflow channel, and delta. The Jezero Route Planner finds the fastest safe rover route between two points the user picks, avoiding steep and rough terrain, extreme cold, dust devils, radiation, and perchlorate-rich soil. Hazards change with the time of day, and if a user picks a dangerous spot, the app explains why, for example “Radiation is too high.” Finally, Survival Expedition is a game where players drive a crewed rover with the mouse to discover five real landmarks while managing battery and food. A green safe-return zone shrinks as resources run down, warnings appear when food drops to 15% and 10%, and each landmark unlocks an achievement that teaches Mars science. The Mission Knowledge Check is a quiz about surviving on Mars. Choosing an answer reveals a short explanation, so players learn from every choice.

How it works

We processed NASA’s controlled HiRISE and CTX mosaics and elevation models of Jezero in QGIS to build the 3D crater terrain. For the 2D tools, we flattened a 3D elevation view into an accurate top-down map by matching 286 features between it and the flat HiRISE photo (SIFT with RANSAC) and computing a perspective transform, with about 1 pixel of error. The map scale, about 17.3 m per pixel, comes from the known size of Belva crater. The map is then divided into a grid of about 10,000 cells, each about 208 m wide, storing height, roughness, temperature, dust, radiation, and perchlorate levels. A cell is blocked if any value breaks a safety limit, such as an elevation change of 35 m or more within the cell, and a one-cell safety buffer surrounds every hazard. The route planner uses the algorithm,

 f(n) = g(n) + h(n), 

where g is the drive time so far and h is the straight-line distance to the goal divided by the drive speed. Each step costs 

(distance + 3 × climb) / (150 m per sol × speed factor),

 so steep or rough ground is slower, and the algorithm is guaranteed to return the fastest safe route. In the game, Dijkstra’s algorithm calculates the battery and sols needed to return to base from every cell, and a cell stays in the safe zone only if the remaining battery and food can cover that trip.

Benefits and intended impact

The project helps students and the public learn real Mars geography, and why Perseverance went to Jezero, by exploring instead of reading. It also shows how mission planners turn data into decisions using hazard limits, safety margins, and a point of no return, ideas that matter for future crewed missions. The same method could be applied to other landing sites on Mars or the Moon, and because the site clearly labels which data is real and which is simulated, it also teaches good scientific practice. The quiz lets visitors test what they learned after exploring.

Creativity

Visitors move from flying around the whole planet, to exploring Jezero in 3D, to planning a route in 2D, to surviving a mission, all on real NASA data. We recovered a true topographic map from a 3D render with computer vision instead of using a placeholder map. Hazards shift through the day, with cold air pooling in low ground in the morning and dust devils peaking at midday. Blocked spots always explain why, and in the game players can watch their safe area shrink, which makes resource planning visible. The quiz, every answer, right or wrong, teaches something, so it is about learning, not grading.

Factors we considered

We prioritized scientific honesty. The maps, terrain, elevation, and landmarks come from real NASA data, while the temperature, dust, radiation, and perchlorate zones are simulated and scaled to real Perseverance weather measurements, and battery and food values are game settings. We also considered safety margins, realistic rover speed on rough ground, plain-language warnings, hazards shown with patterns as well as colors, and a layout that runs in any browser, including on phones.

Tools and technologies

We built the website in Framer with React code components, using JavaScript, TypeScript, and HTML5 Canvas. We used QGIS to process the HiRISE and CTX data and build the 3D terrain, and Python with NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV, and Pillow for image processing and map alignment. The main algorithms are A* search, Dijkstra’s algorithm, perspective transforms, and grid-based hazard analysis. Claude (Anthropic) helped write and debug the code for the route planner and survival game and process the map images, and Framer AI helped with parts of the site layout. All work was done on personal laptops.
